lesson.title: Reading a Random Digit Table Two Digits at a Time
lesson.summary: A random digit table is a long list of the digits 0 through 9 built so every digit is equally likely at every position and independent of its neighbors, giving a simple, rigorous way to run a simulation or choose a random sample by hand.
lesson.body:
A random digit table is exactly what it sounds like: a long sequence of digits, 0 through 9, generated so that every digit is equally likely to appear in any position, 1 chance in 10 each, and knowing one digit tells you nothing about what comes next. That is the same idea behind a random number generator, just written out on paper instead of produced on demand by a calculator or piece of software. Before computers and calculators could generate random numbers instantly, a printed table like this was the standard tool for running the very simulations described in the last two sections, and working through one by hand is still the clearest way to see exactly what "random" means in practice.

Using the table has a simple procedure. Decide how many digits you need to label each possible outcome, so that every outcome gets an equal length code. Pick a starting point in the table, anywhere will do as long as you did not choose it based on wanting a particular result. Then read off digits in groups of that fixed length, moving left to right. If a group of digits does not correspond to any valid label, skip it and move to the next group. If you are sampling without replacement and a group repeats a label you already used, skip that too.

Here is a worked example. Select a random sample of 3 students from a class of 20, numbered 00 through 19, two digits each. Any two digit group from 20 through 99 is not a valid label and must be skipped. Suppose the table gives this string of digits: 05201 31347 68199 109.

Read two digits at a time from the left: 05, 20, 13, 13, 47, 68, 19, 91, 09. Work through them in order. 05 is between 00 and 19, so select student 05. 20 is outside the valid range, since labels only go up to 19, so skip it. 13 is valid, so select student 13. The next group is 13 again, which is a valid label but a repeat of a student already chosen, so skip it. 47 and 68 are both outside the valid range, so skip both. 19 is valid, so select student 19. At this point three distinct students have been selected: 05, 13, and 19, which is exactly the sample size needed, so the process stops there without reading any further digits.

The same skip and reject logic scales up to any simulation: assign digit codes so their proportions match the real probabilities, read the table in fixed size chunks, and discard anything that falls outside your labeling scheme or repeats when it should not.
